short_definition: Double-entry bookkeeping is an accounting system in which every transaction is recorded in at least two accounts — a debit and an equal credit — so the books always balance.
explanation: Double-entry bookkeeping rests on the accounting equation: assets = liabilities + equity. Every transaction is recorded as a debit in one account and an equal credit in another, so total debits always equal total credits. Debits increase asset and expense accounts. Credits increase liability, equity and revenue accounts.

The matching entries give you a built-in error check and produce the figures for the balance sheet and income statement. Most accounting software applies double-entry rules behind the scenes, even when you just categorize transactions.

The trade-off is complexity. Debits and credits feel backwards at first, and balanced books are not necessarily correct, because an entry posted to the wrong account still balances. Record-keeping requirements for small businesses differ by country, so check with your tax authority or an accountant.
example: Example (illustrative numbers): A freelancer invoices a client $1,500. Entry 1: debit Accounts Receivable $1,500, credit Revenue $1,500. When the client pays, entry 2: debit Cash $1,500, credit Accounts Receivable $1,500. Each entry balances, and the receivable drops back to zero.
common_mistake: Assuming a debit always means money going out and a credit means money coming in, as on a bank statement. In bookkeeping a debit increases asset and expense accounts, and your bank statement shows the bank's side of the books, which is reversed.
title: Double-Entry Bookkeeping
